prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Figure 7.1-4 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Business Format Guidance b. Permissive: mainly fast-food dining businesses and various small- and medium-scale retail businesses. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Figure 7.1-5 Schematic Diagram of Permissive Business Format Guidance c. Prohibited: mainly various flavor-style dining businesses. Roundabouts** A. Conventional roundabouts should not be used at urban arterial road intersections. For roads approaching an intersection on a grade, when the longitudinal gradient is ≥3%, a roundabout at-grade intersection should not be adopted. Roundabout at-grade intersections shall not be used on expressways or on major arterials with heavy traffic volumes. B. The number of motor-vehicle lanes in the roundabout should preferably be arranged as 2 to 3 lanes. For the reconstruction of existing large roundabouts or where special needs exist, the requirements may be relaxed. **2.2.6 Sight Distance Requirements** Landscaping and greenery within the sight triangle of at-grade intersections shall remain visually open and unobstructed. Obstacles that obstruct the driver’s line of sight within the sight triangle of an at-grade intersection shall be removed. Greenery higher than 1.2 m that obstructs the driver’s line of sight is not permitted. **2.3 Grade-separated Intersections** When expressways intersect with urban roads of all classes, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with expressways, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with arterial roads, grade-separated intersections shall be adopted. The conditions for setting up grade-separated crossings between roads and railways are as follows: A. Grade-separated intersections must be provided where expressways cross railways. B. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads, secondary arterial roads, and branch roads cross railways and where traffic volume at the crossing is high or railway shunting operations are frequent and the cumulative closure time of the crossing is long. C. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads and secondary arterial roads cross railways and where, during peak road traffic periods, long single-closure periods occur frequently. D. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where roads used by trams or trolleybuses cross railways. 35 **2.4 Roads** **2.4.1 New Construction Projects** Urban road traffic design shall follow the following principles: 1. People-oriented: importance shall be attached to the functional requirements of urban roads in shaping the environment and enhancing road vitality, and importance shall be attached to road landscape design with natural and humanistic features to create a pleasant road traffic environment. 2. System coordination: the designed road shall be incorporated into the overall urban road network, with full consideration of land-use functions and traffic characteristics within the road influence area, so as to achieve integration and coordination between land use functions and the transport system. 3. Functional matching: due consideration shall be given to the various use functions and attributes of roads, and the functional spatial requirements of various transport modes in the higher-level plan shall be coordinated and implemented, while meeting the needs of public activity space. 4. Safety and order: traffic safety hazards shall be reduced through facility layout, engineering, and management measures, with particular emphasis on protecting vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists, and ensuring orderly traffic flow. 5. prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):
{
"scores": {
"justice": {
"overall": 68.0,
"equity": 70.0,
"fairness": 60.0,
"accessibility": 75.0
},
"safety": 72.0,
"livability": 65.0,
"sustainability": 58.0,
"aesthetics": 80.0,
"comfort": 62.0,
"walkability": 70.0
},
"explanations": {
"justice": [
"Wide sidewalks and ramps improve accessibility",
"Lack of tactile paving reduces fairness for visually impaired users",
"Sidewalk width is suitable for wheelchairs, reflecting equitable distribution"
],
"safety": [
"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",
"Limited visible lighting may reduce nighttime safety",
"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],
"livability": [
"Ground-floor commercial units and visible activity indicate a vibrant environment",
"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],
"sustainability": [
"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"
],
"aesthetics": [
"Uniform building heights and consistent facade designs create visual coherence",
"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",
"Appropriate greenery embellishments enhance visual appeal"
],
"comfort": [
"Sparse tree coverage and lack of shading facilities may lead to thermal discomfort in hot weather",
"Lack of benches or resting points reduces comfort for elderly pedestrians",
"Wide, flat sidewalk surfaces support comfortable walking",
"Low traffic noise provides good acoustic comfort"
],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",
"Frequent crossings and curb ramps improve route connectivity",
"Street-level shade and frontage activity increase walking comfort and attractiveness"
]
}
}
 5. Quality Redlines:
1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.

Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Roundabouts** A. Conventional roundabouts should not be used at urban arterial road intersections. For roads approaching an intersection on a grade, when the longitudinal gradient is ≥3%, a roundabout at-grade intersection should not be adopted. Roundabout at-grade intersections shall not be used on expressways or on major arterials with heavy traffic volumes. B. The number of motor-vehicle lanes in the roundabout should preferably be arranged as 2 to 3 lanes. For the reconstruction of existing large roundabouts or where special needs exist, the requirements may be relaxed. **2.2.6 Sight Distance Requirements** Landscaping and greenery within the sight triangle of at-grade intersections shall remain visually open and unobstructed. Obstacles that obstruct the driver’s line of sight within the sight triangle of an at-grade intersection shall be removed. Greenery higher than 1.2 m that obstructs the driver’s line of sight is not permitted. **2.3 Grade-separated Intersections** When expressways intersect with urban roads of all classes, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with expressways, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with arterial roads, grade-separated intersections shall be adopted. The conditions for setting up grade-separated crossings between roads and railways are as follows: A. Grade-separated intersections must be provided where expressways cross railways. B. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads, secondary arterial roads, and branch roads cross railways and where traffic volume at the crossing is high or railway shunting operations are frequent and the cumulative closure time of the crossing is long. C. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads and secondary arterial roads cross railways and where, during peak road traffic periods, long single-closure periods occur frequently. D. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where roads used by trams or trolleybuses cross railways. 35 **2.4 Roads** **2.4.1 New Construction Projects** Urban road traffic design shall follow the following principles: 1. People-oriented: importance shall be attached to the functional requirements of urban roads in shaping the environment and enhancing road vitality, and importance shall be attached to road landscape design with natural and humanistic features to create a pleasant road traffic environment. 2. System coordination: the designed road shall be incorporated into the overall urban road network, with full consideration of land-use functions and traffic characteristics within the road influence area, so as to achieve integration and coordination between land use functions and the transport system. 3. Functional matching: due consideration shall be given to the various use functions and attributes of roads, and the functional spatial requirements of various transport modes in the higher-level plan shall be coordinated and implemented, while meeting the needs of public activity space. 4. Safety and order: traffic safety hazards shall be reduced through facility layout, engineering, and management measures, with particular emphasis on protecting vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists, and ensuring orderly traffic flow. 5.
